steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Tawhid is the central belief of Islam — there is only one God (Allah), with no partners, equals or divisions. It is the first part of the Shahadah: "There is no god but Allah." Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) expresses tawhid: "He is Allah, the One and Only."

steps.title: Exam Tip
steps.body: Tawhid influences every aspect of Muslim life: it forbids shirk (associating partners with God), which is the greatest sin in Islam. This is why Muslims reject the Christian Trinity (they see it as shirk) and why images of Allah or Muhammad are forbidden in mosques (to prevent idolatry).

steps.title: RS Exam Tips — Tawhid: The Oneness of God
steps.body: 1. For Tawhid: The Oneness of God questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Tawhid: The Oneness of God to its real-world impact on believers and society

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: The Qur’an describes Allah’s creative power: “He it is who has created the heavens and the earth in six days and His Throne was upon the waters” (Surah 11:7). For Muslims, the natural world — its beauty, complexity and order — is evidence of Allah’s existence and power, inspiring gratitude and worship.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the nature of Allah. | "Tawhid is the most important Muslim belief." Evaluate this statement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to specific sources of authority (scripture, sacred texts, religious leaders) Explain contrasting beliefs — different views within and between traditions Use key terminology precisely (e.g. tawhid, atonement, sanctity of life) For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider both sides before reaching a justified conclusion Link beliefs to their impact on individuals, communities and society Acknowledge diversity — no religious tradition has a single, uniform view
